Async Rust is the part most people bounce off. The core idea is small; the ecosystem around it is large. This module builds the mental model first, then shows the patterns you will actually write.

The mental model

An async fn returns a future: a value representing work that has not happened yet. A future does nothing until something polls it. A runtime (tokio, async-std, smol) drives the polling.

Compare with threads: spawning a thread starts it. Calling an async fn starts nothing. That difference is why you must .await or hand the future to a runtime.

Future is a trait

poll returns Ready(value) when done, Pending when it is waiting. The runtime registers a waker and sleeps the thread until something is ready. That is how one thread handles thousands of connections: it is never blocked, it is only ever waiting.

Rule of thumb: async is about waiting, not about speed. CPU work in an async task blocks the executor and starves every other task on that thread. Use tokio::task::spawn_blocking or rayon for that.

Tokio setup

features = ["full"] is convenient for learning; in production list only what you use — it cuts compile time noticeably.

#[tokio::main] is sugar for building a multi-threaded runtime and blocking on the future. For more control:

Concurrency: join!, try_join!, spawn

Tool Meaning
.await in sequence run one after another
join! run all, wait for all
try_join! run all, return early on first error
spawn run on the runtime, independent lifetime
spawn_blocking run blocking code on a dedicated thread pool
select! wait for the first to complete

Gotcha: select! cancels by dropping the losing future. If that future was halfway through a multi-step operation, you get a partial write. Guard non-cancellable work with tokio::spawn (a spawned task is not cancelled when its handle is dropped) or make the operation idempotent.

Blocking inside async

Never call std::thread::sleep in async code — it blocks the whole worker. Use tokio::time::sleep.

Shared state in async

Rule of thumb: use std::sync::Mutex when the lock is held across no .await. Use tokio::sync::Mutex only when you must hold it across an .await — it is slower and it makes deadlocks easier.

Channels:

Send + 'static bounds, and why spawn complains

tokio::spawn needs the future to be Send + 'static: it may run on another thread and may outlive the current frame. Fixes:

Holding a non-Send guard across .await

The error is future cannot be sent between threads safely. The fix is almost always to scope the guard: { let g = ...; ... } ending before the .await.

Pin and why futures are pinned

A future is a state machine, and one state may contain a reference to another. If the future moved in memory, those references would dangle. Pin<&mut F> guarantees the future will not move.

In practice you meet Pin in:

  • Box::pin(fut) when you need a heap-allocated future
  • Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + Send>> in trait-object position
  • error messages about "cannot move out of pinned"

You rarely write Pin by hand.

Streams

An async iterator:

buffer_unordered(10) is the standard answer to "fetch 1000 URLs but only 10 at a time". It is how you avoid both serial slowness and connection exhaustion.

Exercises

  1. Write two async fns sleeping 100 ms and 200 ms. Time a.await; b.await; vs tokio::join!(a, b). Confirm ~300 ms vs ~200 ms.
  2. Add a 50 ms timeout to a 200 ms operation with tokio::time::timeout and handle the Elapsed error.
  3. Deliberately call std::thread::sleep inside an async task running on a 1-worker runtime alongside a ticker, and observe the ticker stalling. Fix it.
  4. Fetch 100 fake URLs with buffer_unordered(10) and compare against a sequential loop.
  5. Implement an async fn in a trait with + Send in the return position and spawn it.
  6. Explain the compiler error when a RefCell borrow guard lives across an .await in a spawned task.
